report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: User Engagement Strategies for Digital Medication Adherence Interventions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

text.text: Background: Medication adherence is critical for chronic disease management, yet poor adherence remains an unsolved challenge.
Digital health interventions are promising to support medication adherence but are limited by poor user engagement with the tools.
Understanding which strategies effectively support user engagement could improve the efficacy and sustainability of these interventions.

Purpose: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized strategies used to support user engagement in digital adherence interventions with the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy and evaluated whether these strategies were associated with medication adherence and user engagement outcomes.

Methods: Electronic databases (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, and Web of Science Core Collection) were searched (4/18/2025) to identify randomized controlled trials of app-based digital adherence interventions for people with chronic medical conditions taking oral medications, published in English between 2020 and 2025.
User engagement strategies were characterized with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy.
Meta-regression models evaluated associations between specific techniques and study outcomes.
Risk of bias was characterized with the Risk of Bias-1 measure.
Results: The 60 studies included for review predominantly included adults with cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes (median N=117, IQR=72.0-204.5).
All but one included at least one user engagement strategy appropriate to characterize with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy.

The most common techniques were Prompts/cues (90%), Instruction on how to perform the behavior (70%), Adding objects to the environment (35%), Feedback on behavior (28%), Self-monitoring of behavior (25%), Credible source (22%), Goal setting (behavior) (20%), and Self-monitoring outcome(s) of behavior (20%).
Prompts/cues were frequently paired with another behavior change technique (54%).
User engagement was rarely measured as an outcome, and thus, it was not possible to evaluate this outcome in the metaanalysis.
In the 44 studies included in the meta-analysis of medication adherence outcomes, there were no statistically significant associations with user engagement techniques.

Conclusions: Digital adherence interventions commonly include strategies to support user engagement, particularly prompts/cues, but it remains unknown whether these strategies translate to actual user engagement.
No user engagement strategy was associated with medication adherence outcomes.
This may reflect variability across study samples and medication adherence measurement approaches, threats to internal validity, or reliance on ineffective strategies.
Further research should continue to evaluate which engagement strategies support sustained digital adherence tool use and improved adherence outcomes.

: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Medication adherence, or the extent to which a person's medication-taking behavior aligns with their prescribed regimen [1], is essential for effective long-term management of chronic disease [2].
However, poor medication adherence is extremely common [3], with at least 50% of patients demonstrating suboptimal adherence [2].
Nonadherence has consistently been linked to accelerated disease progression, poorer health outcomes, increased hospitalizations, and higher healthcare costs [4-6].
For many patients, adherence is complicated by personal barriers, such as forgetfulness, limited social support, and complexity of managing multiple medications.
Adherence promotion interventions are critically needed to help patients overcome barriers, consistently take medicine, and support positive health outcomes [7].
Digital health interventions are promising tools to support medication adherence and disease self-management [8-10].

Digital health involves the use of information and communication technologies, such as wearable and non-wearable devices, smartphone apps, and text messaging [9], to help people manage illness and promote wellness [11].
These tools have the potential to help patients more easily engage in their own care [9], by providing real-time adherence intervention and support integrated in patients' daily home routines.
Moreover, over 90% of Americans own a smartphone, indicating that digital health interventions could help increase access to empirically-supported adherence-promoting strategies [12].
However, a major limitation of digital health interventions is poor user engagement with these tools [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18].

text.text: User engagement includes both behavioral engagement, or interactions with and use of the technology, and the subjective experience of using the intervention tools [19, 20].

text.text: Thus, if behavioral engagement with a digital health intervention is inconsistent or insufficient, users may not experience meaningful adherence benefit.
However, little is known about how to best support sustained use of digital health tools, or how much engagement is necessary to produce behavioral or health benefit [18, 21, 22].

text.text: Consistent with the limited empirical literature on user engagement with digital health tools, including those targeting medication adherence [21], the specific strategies used to support behavioral engagement remain poorly understood.

text.text: Characterizing user engagement strategies in existing digital adherence interventions could help to identify which techniques are most effective.

Specifically, applying the Behavior Change Technique taxonomy, a standardized framework of 93 discrete techniques [23], to existing digital adherence interventions may help identify which strategies have been used to support user engagement and whether they are associated with better medication adherence and engagement outcomes.

text.text: To our knowledge, the Behavior Change Technique taxonomy has not been used to characterize strategies for supporting user engagement in digital adherence interventions.

Thus, the objectives of this systematic review and meta-analysis are to answer the following research questions: (1) what proportion of user-facing digital adherence interventions for people with chronic medical conditions include strategies to support user engagement with digital tools?

text.text: (2) which behavior change techniques characterize the user engagement strategies used in these interventions?
(3) do interventions with user engagement strategies have stronger effects on medication adherence and user engagement outcomes than those that do not?
and (4) which user engagement strategies (characterized as behavior change techniques) are associated with stronger effects on medication adherence and user engagement outcomes?

This systematic review and meta-analysis was preregistered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (registration number masked for review) and conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis) guidelines [24].

text.text: The review team, comprised of the Principal Investigator (masked for review) and five Research Assistants (masked for review), established a standardized workflow documented in a Manual of Operating Procedures for literature screening and data extraction.
This systematic review and meta-analysis of published research studies did not require Institutional Review Board approval.
The search strategy was developed by the Principal Investigator and an Informationist at the (masked for review) Library.

The databases searched include the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, and Web of Science Core Collection, restricted to manuscripts published between 2020-2025 (date of search: 4/18/2025).
See Supplemental Figure 1 for search query details.
text.formatted: See Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for search query details.

text.text: Manuscripts were evaluated for the following inclusion criteria: (1) empirical study involving original data collection, (2) evaluation of a digital health intervention in a randomized controlled trial, (3) intervention targeted oral medication adherence, which was quantitatively measured, (4) intervention was used by people managing a chronic medical condition and/or their caregivers, and (5) the study was published in a peer-reviewed journal between 2020-2025.

Although user engagement was a main outcome of interest, we included studies that did not quantitatively measure user engagement if all other inclusion criteria were met given that user engagement is not consistently measured in digital health research [21].
text.formatted: Although user engagement was a main outcome of interest, we included studies that did not quantitatively measure user engagement if all other inclusion criteria were met given that user engagement is not consistently measured in digital health research <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Exclusion criteria were (1) not published in a peer-reviewed journal, (2) not available in English, (3) not published between 2020-2025, (4) does not include participants following an oral medication regimen for a chronic medical condition (excludes acute illness and short course medication regimens), (5) does not evaluate a patient or caregiver-facing digital health intervention for adherence promotion (excluded interventions used by healthcare providers only), (6) single group experimental design, qualitative-only or descriptive only study, (7) systematic review, metaanalysis, think piece, conference abstract, or published protocol.
text.formatted: Exclusion criteria were (1) not published in a peer-reviewed journal, (2) not available in English, (3) not published between 2020-2025, (4) does not include participants following an oral medication regimen for a chronic medical condition (excludes acute illness and short course medication regimens), <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> does not evaluate a patient or caregiver-facing digital health intervention for adherence promotion (excluded interventions used by healthcare providers only), (6) single group experimental design, qualitative-only or descriptive only study, (7) systematic review, metaanalysis, think piece, conference abstract, or published protocol.

text.text: Citations returned from the search strategy were imported into Covidence [25], an online collaborative platform for streamlined systematic review and meta-analysis study selection and data extraction.
text.formatted: Citations returned from the search strategy were imported into Covidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, an online collaborative platform for streamlined systematic review and meta-analysis study selection and data extraction.

text.text: Duplicate citations were removed, followed by title and abstract screening and full-text review (detailed below).
At each level of review, manuscripts were evaluated by two blinded review team members.
Discrepancies were resolved through discussions between the Principal Investigator and review team members at regular research meetings.
Title and Abstract Screening.
Titles and abstracts were reviewed to identify manuscripts that appeared to meet inclusion criteria or needed further investigation to determine qualification at the full-text review phase.
Manuscripts that clearly did not meet inclusion criteria were excluded at this screening stage.
The review team conducted a full-text review of all studies that appeared to meet inclusion criteria based on the title and abstract screening phase to confirm if inclusion criteria were met.
Manuscripts meeting inclusion criteria at this level of review progressed to the Data Extraction phase and were included in the final systematic review and meta-analysis.

The review team extracted key participant and intervention characteristics, quantitative measures of medication adherence and user engagement, and, when available, data necessary for calculating a standardized effect size (e.g., mean, standard deviation).
Any data that were unavailable or not reported were coded as "999" or "no/not reported."
Medication adherence was operationalized as the extent to which a person followed their prescribed oral medication regimen.

User engagement was operationalized as users' behavioral interactions with or use of the intervention technology (i.e., how often a user logs into the app or module completion) rather than the subjective experience of interacting with the technology [20, 26].
text.formatted: User engagement was operationalized as users' behavioral interactions with or use of the intervention technology (i.e., how often a user logs into the app or module completion) rather than the subjective experience of interacting with the technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref>.

text.text: If the study authors described discrete strategies to support behavioral user engagement and interaction with the digital adherence intervention, the review team characterized the strategies with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy [23] following a decision algorithm developed by the Principal Investigator and review team.
text.formatted: If the study authors described discrete strategies to support behavioral user engagement and interaction with the digital adherence intervention, the review team characterized the strategies with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> following a decision algorithm developed by the Principal Investigator and review team.

text.text: Reviewers first determined whether the intervention supported, elicited, or encouraged behavioral engagement or interactions with any component of the digital health tools, such as prompting users to enter medication adherence data in an app or setting weekly app usage goals.

If the intervention supported, elicited, or encouraged behavioral engagement or interactions with the digital health tools, the review team characterized the strategies used to support user engagement using the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy.
Multiple behavior change techniques could be assigned to an intervention.

After independent reviewer coding, behavior change technique assignments underwent additional review for accuracy and agreement by the Principal Investigator and two other team members (masked for review), and discrepancies were resolved through group discussion.

For each included study, the methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias-1 tool (ROB1) [27], which evaluates six domains: selection bias (random sequence generation and allocation concealment), performance bias (blinding of participants and personnel), detection bias (blinding of outcome assessors), attrition bias (incomplete outcome data), reporting bias (selective outcome reporting), and other potential sources of bias not captured in the other domains.
text.formatted: For each included study, the methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias-1 tool (ROB1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>, which evaluates six domains: selection bias (random sequence generation and allocation concealment), performance bias (blinding of participants and personnel), detection bias (blinding of outcome assessors), attrition bias (incomplete outcome data), reporting bias (selective outcome reporting), and other potential sources of bias not captured in the other domains.

text.text: Each study was independently assessed by two blinded coders, with discrepancies resolved by the review team in consultation with the Principal Investigator to characterize the risk of bias.

Studies were characterized as (1) meeting all criteria; (2) failing to meet one criterion or had at least two criteria rated as "unclear" but were considered unlikely to have introduced significant bias; or (3) failing to meet at least one criterion or had at least two criteria that were "unclear" and likely introduced significant bias.
Additional information was not sought by the review team if the study authors' reporting was unclear or unavailable in the manuscript.

Given that this systematic review and meta-analysis focused on user engagement strategies rather than overall intervention effectiveness, no further certainty assessment beyond risk of bias was conducted.
Study characteristics were descriptively reported (frequencies, percentages).
When available, standardized effect sizes were calculated for medication adherence and user engagement outcomes to measure the magnitude of difference between randomized groups.

Effect sizes were initially expressed as Hedges' g or log odds ratios depending on the available outcome data; log odds ratio effect sizes were then converted to Hedges' g to provide a standardized effect size comparable across studies.
When studies reported multiple outcomes, the primary medication adherence or user engagement outcome was selected for effect size calculation.
If no primary outcome was identified, the outcome that was objectively measured was selected first, followed by the outcome most directly reflective of medication adherence or user engagement.
If outcomes were measured at multiple time points, the measurement closest to the end of the intervention phase was selected.

These effect sizes were used in the planned random-effects models to evaluate whether intervention effects differed between interventions targeting user engagement versus not and by user engagement-behavior change technique used.
Publication bias was characterized using a funnel plot.
Heterogeneity was characterized with the I² test and 95% confidence intervals were reported as appropriate.
Data analyses were conducted in RStudio with the metafor package [28].

text.text: The initial search returned 2,313 studies, of which 1,020 duplicate citations were removed.
During title and abstract screening, 1,142 studies were removed (did not meet inclusion criteria) resulting in 151 studies that underwent full-text review.
Of these 151 studies, 91 (60%) were excluded because the study was a conference abstract, pre-print, or protocol only.

Other reasons for exclusion were that the intervention, outcomes, patient population, or study design did not meet inclusion criteria or the manuscript was not available in English, resulting in 60 studies included in the systematic review (see Supplemental File 1 for all included studies and key characteristics).

Of these 60 studies, only three quantitatively measured user engagement and reported sufficient data for effect size calculation, thus it was not possible to evaluate user engagement effects by user engagement-behavior change technique.
For medication adherence, 45 (75%) studies reported data appropriate for effect size calculation; however, one study was a significant outlier [29] and was, therefore, excluded from meta-analysis.
text.formatted: For medication adherence, 45 (75%) studies reported data appropriate for effect size calculation; however, one study was a significant outlier <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> and was, therefore, excluded from meta-analysis.

text.text: Thus, 44 studies were included in the meta-analysis of medication adherence outcomes.
See Figure 1 for a flow diagram of the initial search, screening, and reasons for exclusion.

text.text: Out of the 60 studies included in this systematic review, 75% (n=45) were performed outside of the United States.
Consistent with the inclusion criteria, all studies were randomized controlled trials.
The median sample size at randomization was 117 (IQR 72.0-204.5), and the median sample size allocated to the treatment group was 57.5 (IQR 35.0-102.0).
The most common medical conditions were cardiovascular and related diseases (n=12, 20%), hypertension (n=11, 18%) Type 2 Diabetes (n=9, 15%), cancer (n=7, 12%), and HIV (n=7, 12%).
Consistent with inclusion criteria, all included studies evaluated an app-based intervention.
Over half involved human support to engage with the intervention (n=37, 62%).
Only 20% (n=12) reported providing incentives for study participation.
See Table 1 for more details.

text.text: Nearly all the studies (n=56, 93%) failed to meet at least one risk of bias assessment criterion or had at least two criteria that were "unclear" and likely introduced significant bias, primarily due to challenges blinding participants and personnel to intervention group assignment.
The remaining four (7%) studies failed to meet one criterion or had at least two criteria rated as "unclear" but were considered unlikely to have introduced significant bias.

As a sensitivity analysis to remove blinding from the assessment criteria, 67% (n=40) still failed to meet at least one risk of bias assessment criterion or had at least two criteria that were unclear and likely introduced bias, 30% (n=18) failed to meet one criterion or had at least two criteria rated as "unclear" but were considered unlikely to have introduced bias, and 3% (n=2) met all criteria (low risk of bias).
Nearly all included studies (n=59, 98%) described at least one strategy to support user engagement with the digital health tools.

Characterizing these strategies with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy [23], the most common techniques were Prompts/cues (n=54, 90%), Instructions on how to perform the behavior (n=42, 70%), and Feedback on behavior (n=17, 28%), See Table 2 for a complete list of user engagement-behavior change techniques with representative examples.

text.text: Prompts/cues were occasionally paired with another behavior change technique (n=29 out of 54 studies with Prompts/cues (54%)).

Of these 29 studies, the most common combination was Prompts/cues + Self-monitoring of behavior (n=12, 41%), followed by Self-monitoring of outcomes of behavior (n=10, 34.48%), Credible source (n=6, 21%), Biofeedback (n=6, 21%), and Social support (unspecified) (n=5, 17%).

text.text: For medication adherence, the mean standardized effect size was 0.55 (95% CI=0.22-0.88; p=0.001; see Supplemental Figure 2 for a forest plot of study effect sizes) indicating that participants randomized to the digital adherence intervention group had significantly higher improvement in medication adherence compared to participants in the comparator group.

text.text: High heterogeneity was observed across the trials (I² =97.54%).

Publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of a funnel plot (see Supplement Figure 3), revealing some asymmetry likely reflecting that smaller studies with positive results were more likely to be published than smaller studies with non-statistically significant or negative results.
text.formatted: Publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of a funnel plot (see Supplement Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>), revealing some asymmetry likely reflecting that smaller studies with positive results were more likely to be published than smaller studies with non-statistically significant or negative results.

text.text: We were not able to evaluate whether interventions containing strategies to support user engagement had stronger effects on medication adherence or user engagement compared to those that did not because all but one study described at least one discrete user engagement strategy (n=59, 98%).

Given that some user engagement-behavior change techniques appeared in a small number of studies, meta-regression models only were evaluated for techniques appearing in >18% of studies (Prompts/cues, Instruction on how to perform the behavior, Feedback on behavior, Self-monitoring of behavior, Credible source, Adding objects to the environment, Goal setting (behavior), Self-monitoring of outcome(s) of behavior, Biofeedback).

text.text: These models revealed no significant differences on medication adherence effects based on whether the user engagement-behavior change technique was part of the intervention versus not.

In addition, a meta-regression comparing studies that used Prompts/cues alone to studies pairing Prompts/cues with another behavior change technique did not show a significant difference in medication adherence effects (95% CI=-0.47-1.05; p=0.45).

text.text: Further, little is known about how to optimally support user engagement with digital adherence tools to, in turn, support improved medication adherence or sustained use of the tools [21, 31, 32].
text.formatted: Further, little is known about how to optimally support user engagement with digital adherence tools to, in turn, support improved medication adherence or sustained use of the tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to address this gap as the first to characterize the discrete strategies used to support user engagement with digital adherence interventions, using the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy [23], and to evaluate whether these strategies were associated with stronger effects on medication adherence and user engagement outcomes.
text.formatted: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to address this gap as the first to characterize the discrete strategies used to support user engagement with digital adherence interventions, using the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>, and to evaluate whether these strategies were associated with stronger effects on medication adherence and user engagement outcomes.

text.text: Nearly all studies reviewed incorporated at least one strategy to encourage user engagement, which enabled us to systematically characterize these strategies as discrete behavior change techniques [23].
text.formatted: Nearly all studies reviewed incorporated at least one strategy to encourage user engagement, which enabled us to systematically characterize these strategies as discrete behavior change techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: The most common technique was Prompts/cues, often as push notifications and text messages, which served as reminders for users to engage with the digital adherence intervention.

Over half combined Prompts/cues with another behavior change technique (e.g., delivering a push notification prompting the user to record taking their daily medication dose in the app (self-monitoring of behavior)).
Given that inclusion criteria required the intervention to include a smartphone app, it is not surprising that features intrinsic to smartphones, like push notifications and text messages, dominated.

Instructions on how to perform the behavior, typically in the form of structured guidance (human, video, in-app) on how to navigate and use the digital tools after enrolling in the study, was also common.
Onboarding and uptake challenges are well-known in digital health tools regardless of behavioral target [13, 14, [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Onboarding and uptake challenges are well-known in digital health tools regardless of behavioral target <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it may be beneficial to support users' success with using the tools from the start, thereby helping to support continued engagement.

Notably, over one-third of reviewed studies incorporated Adding objects to the environment by providing participants with a connected device, such as an electronic pill bottle or Bluetooth blood pressure monitor, to use at home.
Integrating devices into participant's home environments may help make the intervention more visible and accessible.

In turn, this strategy could encourage more consistent engagement and provide an alternative digital health-based approach to promoting intervention engagement beyond push notifications or text messages.
Other frequently used techniques included Feedback on behavior, Self-monitoring of behavior, Credible source, Goal setting (behavior), and Self-monitoring of outcome(s) of behavior.

These techniques, as well as Prompt/cues, overlap with those identified in effective digital adherence and self-management interventions [10], highlighting similarities in strategies designed to both promote engagement with the technology itself and strategies intended to target engagement in treatment adherence and self-management behavior(s).
text.formatted: These techniques, as well as Prompt/cues, overlap with those identified in effective digital adherence and self-management interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, highlighting similarities in strategies designed to both promote engagement with the technology itself and strategies intended to target engagement in treatment adherence and self-management behavior(s).

text.text: It is important to note that this review characterized strategies intended to support behavioral engagement with the digital intervention tools, but some strategies, such as Prompts/cues, may have concurrently served as a reminder to take medication.

This duality is important to consider in digital health intervention development, particularly to clearly delineate techniques functioning to support user engagement with the digital tools, taking medicine or engaging in self-management behaviors, or both.
Less than 10% of studies used rewards or incentives to encourage engagement with digital health tools.
This may reflect practical and financial challenges of providing compensation for digital tool use.

It is also possible that relatively small engagement behaviors, such as logging into an app or using a daily electronic pillbox, are not sufficiently motivating targets for small monetary rewards, even when rewards and incentives may increase over time with continued user engagement.

Consistent with prior research showing that user engagement has not been regularly evaluated in digital adherence and self-management interventions [21], we were not able to conduct a meta-analysis of user engagement outcomes because very few studies included appropriate outcome measures.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior research showing that user engagement has not been regularly evaluated in digital adherence and self-management interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, we were not able to conduct a meta-analysis of user engagement outcomes because very few studies included appropriate outcome measures.

text.text: Thus, it remains unknown whether the user engagement techniques characterized in this systematic review effectively encourage sustained use of the digital tools.

Compounding this challenge, comparison groups often did not involve a digital intervention (e.g., treatment as usual) indicating a need for intervention engagement measures that are applicable to both digital-and human-delivered modalities.

Despite the common use of strategies to support user engagement with digital tools, none of the techniques evaluated via meta-regression were significantly associated with medication adherence outcomes.

One possible explanation is that reliance on Prompts/cues contributes to "alert fatigue," which occurs when people become desensitized to excessive notifications and alerts and stop responding to them [33, 34].
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that reliance on Prompts/cues contributes to "alert fatigue," which occurs when people become desensitized to excessive notifications and alerts and stop responding to them <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref>.

text.text: Because people are often inundated with push notifications and text messages, digital health notifications may be easily ignored.
This suggests that future digital adherence interventions should advance beyond simple, generic, static push notifications and text messages.
A transformative approach that could reduce alert fatigue is developing prompts that adapt to users' contexts, preferences, and behavior [35, 36].
text.formatted: A transformative approach that could reduce alert fatigue is developing prompts that adapt to users' contexts, preferences, and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36]</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the second most common user engagement-behavior change technique, Instruction on how to perform the behavior, was typically used at the beginning of the study to assist participants with learning how to use the technology; this strategy may be most helpful for initial engagement rather than supporting longer-term medication adherence.
Continued research is needed to understand how to leverage user engagement strategies to also support medication adherence.
This systematic review and meta-analysis has some limitations.
The majority of studies failed to meet all risk of bias criteria primarily due to challenges with blinding.

There was high heterogeneity in medication adherence outcomes across studies, likely reflecting variability in chronic medical conditions represented and differences in how medication adherence was measured.
These are all inherent limitations in digital health and medication adherence research but are important to consider when interpreting findings, particularly the null meta-regression results.

Finally, a limitation of systematic reviews is that research continues to be published during the data extraction process, a challenge compounded by rapid advances in digital health including artificial intelligence (AI) and how AI could affect user engagement.
As such, this field is expected to continue evolving and an updated review will be warranted in the future.

The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis show that digital adherence intervention developers have incorporated a range of strategies aligned with the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy [23], though heavily reliant on Prompts/cues, to encourage user engagement with the tools.
text.formatted: The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis show that digital adherence intervention developers have incorporated a range of strategies aligned with the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>, though heavily reliant on Prompts/cues, to encourage user engagement with the tools.

text.text: However, it remains unknown which strategies optimally support both user engagement with the tools or improved medication adherence, a critical gap warranting further empirical investigation.

Notably, AI, which was not part of any user engagement strategy characterized in this review, is increasingly integrated into digital health interventions [37] and has potential to transform engagement strategies (e.g., AIpersonalized prompts/cues and proactive feedback about behavior or outcomes of behavior).
text.formatted: Notably, AI, which was not part of any user engagement strategy characterized in this review, is increasingly integrated into digital health interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> and has potential to transform engagement strategies (e.g., AIpersonalized prompts/cues and proactive feedback about behavior or outcomes of behavior).

text.text: However, AI may also introduce unintended negative effects on digital health users [38] and does not guarantee increased interactions with the digital tools.
